clue.text: Currently attractive?

parts.note: the current meant is the electric one, and electro- is the prefix that says so
whatever hauls iron filings towards itself is attractive in the physicist's sense

explanation.surface: Somebody who is good-looking at the moment, whatever they may look like later on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currently' is the physicist's current rather than the adverb for right now, and the pull in 'attractive' is on iron, not on people. Read straight, the sentence describes the field itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An electromagnetic field is made by a current and does the attracting, so both words of the clue describe it literally.

clue.text: The last thing you'll see here!

definitions.text: The last thing you'll see here!

parts.note: read straight, a description of whatever stands at the very end of a written line
'here' is the clue in front of you, so look at the character it stops on

explanation.surface: A warning that whatever you are looking at now is the last sight you will get.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' means this clue, and the clue ends on the very piece of punctuation it is describing, so the setter has shown you the answer without spelling a letter of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation mark closes a sentence, so the final character of this clue is at once the definition and the thing defined.

clue.text: Turned up, unsophisticated in French spa town

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning a word up means reading it from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: naive means innocent and unworldly, i.e. unsophisticated

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin arrives at a fashionable French resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reverses NAIVE, which suits a down entry read from the bottom upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Evian-les-Bains is a resort on Lake Geneva in France, famous for its bottled mineral water.

clue.text: Support from unsettled settler

indicators.note: Something unsettled has been shaken out of its place, so these letters will not stay where the clue put them.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the word the shuffle works on

explanation.surface: A pioneer who never managed to settle down.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the contradiction: an unsettled settler is a person who will not stay put, which is exactly what the letters of the word do here.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is the braced A-frame a plank rests on, so it supports a table top or a bridge span.

clue.text: Gold coin tossed over Womble

indicators.note: A tossed coin lands whichever way up it pleases, so the letters it names come down in a fresh order.

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry, the tincture used on a coat of arms
the four letters of the word for money, landed in a new order
o is the cricket scorer's mark for an over of six balls

explanation.surface: A gold coin flipped over the head of a small furry creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like part of the tossing and is a cricket abbreviation standing on its own, which is what makes the last letter so hard to place.
explanation.definitionFit: Orinoco is one of the Wombles of Wimbledon Common, the burrowing television creatures each named after a place on the map.

clue.text: Changed what happened at noon?

parts.note: the hours before midday are the a.m., and midday is where they stop
what the morning did when twelve o'clock arrived

explanation.surface: A question about the event that took place at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is being timed here: the clue asks what the morning itself did at twelve, and the reply to that question goes straight into the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend something is to alter it, usually a text or a law, so 'changed' is the plain past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Lack of commitments, around a hundred spies

indicators.note: To go around something is to close on both sides of it, so one piece wraps the other instead of following it.

parts.note: a person with no ties has nothing holding them to anyone or anywhere
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A footloose life spent circling a hundred secret agents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spies' is the everyday verb — catches sight of — and not the noun that the surface's hundred agents has you expecting.
explanation.definitionFit: To spy something is to catch sight of it, the plain verb sense rather than anything to do with espionage.

clue.text: Only a Brit worried former PM

indicators.note: A worried person cannot keep still, and letters described that way will not stay in the order printed.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, exactly as the clue prints them

explanation.surface: One anxious Briton, alone in a room full of foreigners.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is a joke at the man's expense: a prime minister who took the country to war beside an American president is cut down here to being only a Brit.
explanation.definitionFit: Tony Blair was Prime Minister from 1997 to 2007, so 'former PM' names him by the office he no longer holds.

clue.text: Acton let brother bother sister

indicators.note: To bother someone is to disturb them, and letters disturbed like that come out in a different arrangement.

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder, and Acton Bell was the pen name of the youngest of three novelist sisters

explanation.surface: One sibling standing back while another one pesters a third.
explanation.walkthrough: The three sisters published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, all of them men's names, and it is the eldest of the three that these fifteen letters rearrange into.
explanation.definitionFit: Acton Bell was the pen name of Anne Brontë, whose elder sister Charlotte is the novelist the definition points at.

clue.text: Tree sounding cool for long

indicators.note: Sounding points at the ear rather than the page: what matters is the noise the word makes, not the way it is spelt.

parts.note: cool weather is chilly, and said aloud that is the South American country
to long for something is to pine for it

explanation.surface: A tree that has been fashionable for a very long time.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves come from different worlds — one from the thermometer, one from yearning — and 'for' belongs to the second of them, since you pine for what you long for.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chile pine is the monkey puzzle, the spiky South American conifer planted in Victorian front gardens.

clue.text: Weight gain shed in horse-drawn carriage

parts.note: a ton is a large unit of weight
GAIN loses the letters I and N, the 'in' the clue names

explanation.surface: Weight somebody put on and has now managed to lose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed in' is two instructions in two words, one saying what goes and one saying which letters go, and the surface hides both inside an ordinary story about dieting.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonga is the light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage of India and Pakistan, still seen in country towns.

clue.text: Girl sent back too much food colouring

parts.note: Anna is a girl's name

indicators.note: something sent back returns the way it came, so these letters are read in reverse

parts.note: OTT is short for over the top, meaning excessive

explanation.surface: A girl returns a dish because it has far too much artificial colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: OTT, short for 'over the top', is a common crossword way to say 'too much'; 'sent back' turns it round after the girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Annatto is an orange-red dye from achiote seeds, used to colour cheese and other foods.

clue.text: Sound measure could be credible — not right!

indicators.note: says the letters of the following word could be arranged into something else
says that a letter must be left out of the fodder before rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone doubts that a claimed noise level is believable.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of CREDIBLE; 'not right' removes R, and 'could be' rearranges the remaining DECIBLE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A decibel is the unit used to express loudness, so it is a measure of sound.

clue.text: Rod's letter is spoken of

indicators.note: Spoken of asks for the sound of the thing rather than its written form, so say it aloud and write down what you hear.

parts.note: the seventeenth letter of the alphabet, whose name takes three letters to write down

explanation.surface: Somebody discussing a letter that belongs to a man called Rod.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rod' is capitalised only because it opens the clue, and it is not a man's name at all but a plain noun doing the whole of the defining.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is the long tapering rod a snooker or billiards player strikes the ball with.

clue.text: C20th style affected trade company

indicators.note: An affected manner is not the natural one, so these letters are put on in an order other than their own.

parts.note: the five letters of the word for business, rearranged
co. is the standard abbreviation after a firm's name

explanation.surface: A trading company that puts on airs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affected' is also the setter's wink at a style its critics called mannered; as an instruction it reaches only as far as the word beside it, and the firm is added afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Art deco is the geometric decorative style of the 1920s and 1930s, so 'C20th style' dates it by its century.

clue.text: Fruit perplexed generations — not so!

indicators.note: something perplexed is muddled, so the letters are jumbled
tells us some letters are to be left out of the fodder before the jumble

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Generations are baffled by a piece of fruit, or perhaps they deny being baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: From GENERATIONS, 'not so' removes S and O, leaving GENERATIN, which 'perplexed' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A tangerine is a small loose-skinned citrus fruit, a kind of mandarin orange.

clue.text: Canoe from which falls an athlete

indicators.note: something falling out of the canoe is removed from it, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tumbles out of a canoe, and that someone is a sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from which falls' takes AN out of CANOE to leave the answer. Seb Coe is a British Olympic middle-distance champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Sebastian Coe won Olympic gold over 1500 metres, so the name fits a famous runner.

clue.text: Reserved half the area with worker

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, so its second four letters are dropped

parts.note: a district is an area
an ant is the classic worker in crosswords, from the worker ants of a colony

explanation.surface: Part of a region has been set aside for a labourer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserved' looks like 'set aside' but means aloof in manner. 'half' keeps only the first four letters of the area word, and the worker is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A reserved person is cool and aloof in manner, which is what this adjective means of a personality.

clue.text: Fish that is around delta

indicators.note: Going around something means closing on both sides of it, so the short piece ends up in the middle.

parts.note: i.e., short for the Latin id est, is 'that is'
delta is D in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A fish swimming about somewhere near a river delta.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are crossword staples worth keeping: the Latin abbreviation for 'that is', and the radio alphabet where Delta stands in for its own initial.
explanation.definitionFit: An ide is a silver freshwater fish of the carp family, common in northern Europe and also called the orfe.

clue.text: Gives the cold shoulder to Italian fellow cycling

indicators.note: cycling a word moves a letter round from one end to the other, like a wheel turning

parts.note: signore is the Italian for a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: An Italian man out on his bike snubs someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves the first S of SIGNORE to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the cold shoulder is to deliberately pay them no attention, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Two girls touching Australian parakeet

indicators.note: Two things touching are set side by side with nothing between, so the pieces run straight into each other.

parts.note: the first of them is Ros, the short form of Rosalind
the second is Ella, a name in its own right and the tail of several longer ones

explanation.surface: Two girls standing shoulder to shoulder.
explanation.walkthrough: Neither name is signalled beyond the word 'girls', so the way in is to try short women's names against the crossing letters until a pair of them meet.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosella is one of the bright broad-tailed parakeets of Australia, common in gardens along the east coast.

clue.text: Squealed about tune for drink

indicators.note: About here means turned about, so the piece it governs is written in the opposite direction to its ordinary spelling.

parts.note: a tune is an air, and here those three letters are written backwards
an informer who talks to the police has sung

explanation.surface: Somebody squealing about a tune in exchange for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squealed' is the gangster's sense, informing rather than shrieking, and 'about' does turning work instead of meaning 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sangria is the Spanish punch of red wine, fruit and soda, so 'drink' names it by its plainest category.

clue.text: Vicar on lake, musing

parts.note: Rev is the title written in front of a clergyman's name
Erie is one of the five Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A vicar out on a lake, lost in thought.
explanation.walkthrough: Erie is the crossword's lake of choice, four letters and three of them vowels, and the vicar in front of it is a title rather than a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a spell of pleasant daydreaming, which is what musing names as a state of mind.

clue.text: Putin is so reactionary — some back out for composer

indicators.note: Some of the words means part of them, so what is wanted is a run of letters already sitting in the clue.
Back out asks for that run to be lifted in the opposite direction to the way it is printed.

parts.note: seven letters lie in a row across those words, and they are read from the right

explanation.surface: A hard-line view of Putin, with some people quietly withdrawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reactionary' does two jobs at once: it lends its opening letter to the run of hidden letters, and its meaning is the setter's nudge to read them the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville and William Tell, so 'composer' names him by his trade.

clue.text: Furious as flower's name concealed

indicators.note: Something concealed is put out of sight inside something bigger, so the letter goes within the word rather than beside it.

parts.note: a violet is the small purple spring flower
n is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Somebody in a rage because a flower's name is being kept secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is a genuine bloom here, not the crossword's usual trick of a thing that flows, and the name hidden in it is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Violent means marked by great force or fury, so 'furious' is a straight synonym in the sense of uncontrolled rage.

clue.text: Previously Argo had leading role cut

indicators.note: The leading letter of a word is the one at its head, and that single letter is what this instruction picks out.

parts.note: the ship Jason sailed in search of the golden fleece

indicators.note: Cut takes away what has just been named, so the letter singled out is removed from the word before it.

parts.note: the letter at its head is R, and that R is the piece taken out

explanation.surface: A production of Argo that has lost its starring part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading role' is one phrase in the surface and two instructions in the wordplay: find the letter at the head of the second word, and lose it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ago and previously both place something at an earlier time, though ago follows its period — two years ago — where previously stands alone.

clue.text: Composer is otherwise in inn, drunk

indicators.note: one piece is placed within the other
being drunk means staggering about, so the letters of inn are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
else means otherwise, as in 'or else'

explanation.surface: A composer behaves differently when drunk at a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' scrambles INN to NIN, and 'otherwise' goes in it; 'is' is just a link. Carl Nielsen was a Danish composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Nielsen wrote six symphonies and is Denmark's best-known classical musician.

clue.text: T20 batsman as small Canadian woodsman

parts.note: S is the clothing size small
a logger fells trees for timber, the lumberjack of the Canadian forests

explanation.surface: A cricketer likened to a small Canadian lumberjack.
explanation.walkthrough: T20 is Twenty20, the twenty-over game in which batters swing at nearly everything, so the definition wants a hitter rather than a stylist.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogger is a batter who hits hard and without finesse, exactly the type the short cricket format rewards.

clue.text: Good supply of water for seed

parts.note: g is the standard abbreviation for good
the water the sky supplies

explanation.surface: Plenty of water, which is exactly what a seed wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good' is not describing the water at all but handing over a letter, and it is the abbreviation that turns up on a school report.
explanation.definitionFit: A grain is a single seed of a cereal such as wheat or rice, so 'seed' names it by what it is.

clue.text: Heartless Elgar and I confused Shakespearean spirit

indicators.note: confused letters are mixed up, so these are rearranged
without its heart, the central letter of the name is removed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cruel Elgar and the speaker are both bewildered by a ghost from Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' takes the middle G out of ELGAR, leaving ELAR; add I and 'confused' rearranges them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariel is the airy sprite who serves Prospero in The Tempest.

clue.text: Cause trouble, as Adam and Eve did?

definitions.meaning: the idiom for kicking up a violent fuss
the first couple brought up a first son, which is these words read one at a time

explanation.surface: Adam and Eve blamed for starting all the trouble there has ever been.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second half as a joke rather than a dictionary sense: the phrase for an uproar is also, word for word, a description of the world's first parenting.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise Cain is to make a violent fuss; word for word it is also what Adam and Eve did in bringing up their firstborn son.

clue.text: Stay away from far off fortress

parts.note: the keep is the strong central tower of a castle
something far off is a long way from where you stand

explanation.surface: Advice to give a remote castle a wide berth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Far off fortress' looks like one noun phrase with an adjective in front, and the two words are separate pieces that swap places on the way into the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep someone at a distance is to hold them off and stay away from them, the idiom for refusing any closeness.
